title: Headings that are not labels
excerpt: A heading should state the claim of the section. 'Our process' is a label. A line about what happens between the call and the launch is a heading.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band. The shared screen fits a piece about headings that point at a specific claim.
caption: A heading should point at the point. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a heading and a label?
faqs.answer: A label names a category, such as 'Services' or 'Our process.' A heading states the claim of that section, such as what the buyer receives or what happens between the call and the launch. Navigation can use labels. Sections of a page should use headings a skimmer can learn from.

faqs.question: Can a question be a heading?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the section answers it. A heading about how long a first project takes works if the next paragraph gives a shape of the time. A question you do not answer is a tease. Use a question when a buyer would actually ask it, and put the answer in the first sentence, not after a windup.

faqs.question: Do headings affect search results?
faqs.answer: They can. Google's title-link documentation says the system looks at heading elements, the visible title, and other prominent text when it decides the title of a result, so a vague heading is a weak candidate and a descriptive one can help. Write the heading for the reader first. A clear claim serves the reader and the result.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A heading should say the claim of the section. That is the standard for website heading writing. "Our process" is a label. "What happens between the call and the launch" is a heading. The label tells you a bucket exists. The heading tells you what is in it.

Buyers scan headings to decide whether to read. A screen reader user jumps by heading to move through the page. Search systems look at headings too, when they decide how to title a result. One vague line fails all three. You can fix it by saying the thing the section is for.

## A claim you could repeat

Read the heading as a sentence a stranger could quote. If it only names a department of the page, it is a label, and the information is still hiding. Replace it with the decision, the outcome, or the boundary the section actually contains.

"Services" becomes "Design and build for a marketing site, from the first page to the handoff." "About" becomes "A small studio that designs and ships the site with you." "FAQ" becomes a real question. The label can survive in the navigation, where space is short and the destination is the point. The heading on the page has room to speak.

Keep it to one idea. A heading with a comma, a slash, and a second metaphor is two headings competing. Split the section or choose the idea that matters. The paragraph can hold the second thought. The heading should be something a person can hold in their head while they scroll.

Match the confidence of the paragraph. A heading that promises a guarantee the body walks back is worse than a modest heading. Write the heading after the paragraph if you tend to oversell, then make the heading as strong as the evidence and no stronger. The reader who checks will compare them.

## The examples worth rewriting

"Our process" hides a sequence the buyer needs. "What happens between the call and the launch" tells them the section is a timeline of responsibility. Under it, the steps can be short. The heading has already done the framing.

"Why us" is a label that invites puffery. "What you can judge us on before you hire anyone" points at proof. The section then has to offer something judgeable: the work, the way the code is handed over, the way communication actually goes. If you cannot fill that heading, you do not have the section yet.

"Solutions" means nothing. Name the solution. "A site your team can edit without a page builder" is a claim. "Features" can become the three capabilities a buyer compares. Each feature heading states the outcome of that feature, not the internal name of the module.

"Blog" as a page title is a label the search result will also suffer from. Google's documentation on title links says to avoid vague descriptors, and to write concise text that describes the page. The same advice is good writing. "Notes on designing a company site" tells a visitor what the journal is. "Blog" tells them you have a blog, which they can see.

## Levels, and the one title that leads

A page gets one main title. It is the promise of the whole page, and it should look like the promise: larger, first, distinct. Section headings sit under it, clearly smaller, all at the same level if they are peers. Subheadings appear only when a section has real parts. A page where every line is a heading has no headings. It has a poster with too many voices.

Google's title-link guidance says the system uses the title element, the main visual title, heading elements, and other prominent text, and that several headings with the same visual weight make it unclear which one is the title. Give the page a single dominant title. Do not style a kicker, a slogan, and a headline as three equal screams. The tool may pick the wrong one for the result, and the reader will also hesitate.

Use real heading levels in the markup, in order. A design that skips from a giant line to a tiny line by faking it with a bold paragraph will look fine and navigate poorly. The levels are the outline. If the outline is nonsense, the page is hard to move through with a keyboard or a reader. Style the levels. Do not replace them with font-size tricks that leave the outline flat.

Keep labels in the navigation and in form groups, where a category is the right tool. "Email" next to a field is a label, and it should stay a label. Do not write a claim in a field caption. The claim belongs in the heading above the form: "Book a call if you have a site to redesign." The field then asks for the address. Roles, respected, make the page feel calm.

## Questions, steps, and parallel lines

A question heading works when the next sentence answers it. "How long does the first build take?" should be followed by the shape of the time, not by a story about how every project is unique. If you cannot answer, do not ask. A rhetorical question as a heading is a label in costume.

Steps should read as steps. "Agree the scope. Design the key pages. Build and launch." Each one can be a heading if the section under it is real. If the section is one sentence, you have a list, not a set of headings. Use the list. Headings that introduce nothing add length to the scan without adding a map.

Parallel structure helps a set. All claims, or all questions, not a mix, unless the mix is the point. "Speed" next to "What you own" next to "Let's talk" is three kinds of line. The eye cannot compare them. Rewrite until a buyer could read the set as one gesture.

Front-load the specific word. "Launch checklist for a company site" is easier to scan than "A few thoughts before you go live with the thing you have been building." The long version can be the first sentence. The heading should arrive sooner. You are writing for someone whose thumb is already moving.

## How search uses the line, and how it does not

Google generates title links automatically and considers on-page headings as one source. If your title element is vague, stuffed, or boilerplate, the visible heading may be what people see in search. That is a reason to write a real heading. It is not a reason to load the heading with synonyms. The documentation is explicit that repeating keywords so the title looks comprehensive makes the result look spammy to people and to Google.

Write the heading for the buyer on the page. Then check the title element, which can be a little tighter, and make sure it still describes the page. A heading that says the claim and a title tag that says the same claim in fewer words is a healthy pair. A heading written only to harvest a query will sound bent, and the paragraph under it will have to apologize.

Do not expect a heading change to rewrite your results overnight. Google notes that it has to recrawl and reprocess the page, which can take days or weeks. Change the heading because the page is clearer today. The search result can catch up. Chasing the result with weekly rewrites produces the half-empty and inconsistent titles the same documentation warns about.

If several pages share a heading, they will be hard to tell apart in a scan of your own site and in a list of results. "Learn more" as the heading on eight sections is the in-page version of boilerplate. Give each section its claim. Give each page its own title. The reader should know where they are from the line alone.

## An outline test before visual design

Write the outline in a document before you place a single box in Figma. Title, then the section claims, then the one action. Read it to someone who has not been in the project. They should be able to say what the page wants them to do. If they ask "what is this section?", the line is still a label. Rewrite it before you spend a day on layout. Layout will not supply the missing noun.

When the design returns, check that the headings are still the headings. Decorative kickers, oversized pull quotes, and banner text have a way of stealing the outline. The claim should be the strongest line in the section. The decoration can be quieter. If a badge reading "New" is louder than the offer, the hierarchy is inverted.

Revisit the outline when the offer changes. A heading is a maintenance surface, like a price. "Fixed packages for every startup" becomes a lie the day you scope a custom build. Update the line in the same edit as the service. Stale headings are how a careful site starts to sound like it belongs to a previous company.

On Hanabi pages the outline is part of the draft the founder sees early, so the claims can be argued before the type is polished. It is easier to change a line in a document than a line that has already been kerned into a hero. Start there. The site will sound like it knows what it is for.

Look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and read only the lines that introduce each project. A heading is doing its job when those lines alone tell you what the work was.

Specific lines from customers are a different kind of claim, and they fail in a similar way when they stay vague. [Testimonials that are allowed to be specific](/blog/testimonials-that-are-allowed-to-be-specific) is the next piece, on writing a quote a serious buyer can actually use.
